items.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
choices: To replace the origin server entirely so it never has to run
To keep copies of content on servers close to visitors, so most requests don't have to travel to the origin
To encrypt traffic between the browser and the origin
To automatically fix bugs in the origin server's code
items.explanation: A CDN's core job is placing copies of content on distributed edge servers near visitors, so most requests are answered nearby instead of crossing the planet to a single origin. It doesn't replace the origin (which still holds the authoritative data), encrypt traffic (that's TLS's job), or fix code.

Why: a CDN's job is proximity — answering requests near the visitor instead of routing every one to a single distant origin.

items.prompt: A visitor in Tokyo requests a page from a site with edge servers around the world. Which server is most likely to answer that request?
choices: The origin server, always, no matter where it is
A random edge server chosen without regard to location
The edge server nearest to the visitor in Tokyo, if it has a cached copy
Whichever server responded to the visitor's previous, unrelated request
items.explanation: A CDN routes requests to the nearest edge server (PoP) that can serve them, since proximity is what reduces round-trip time. Only if that nearby edge server doesn't have a fresh cached copy does the request travel further, potentially all the way to the origin.

items.prompt: Which of these best describes what an 'edge server' (PoP) is, compared to the origin?
choices: It's a second copy of the entire database, always perfectly in sync
It's a nearby server holding cached copies of responses, not the authoritative source of the data
It's a backup server that only activates when the origin is down
It's a load-testing tool used before launch
items.explanation: An edge server holds cached copies of responses close to visitors — it is not the source of truth (that's the origin) and not a full database replica; it's specifically a cache of previously-served responses, valid for a bounded window of time.

items.prompt: A browser has a fresh cached copy of an image. In what order would a request for that image actually be attempted?
choices: It goes straight to the origin, bypassing all caches
It never leaves the browser — the browser cache answers it directly
It goes to the CDN edge first, then falls back to the browser cache
It goes to the origin first, which tells the browser to use its cache
items.explanation: If the browser's own cache already holds a fresh copy, the request is answered locally and never leaves the device at all — it doesn't even reach the CDN edge, let alone the origin. Each layer only gets asked if the layer 'in front' of it (closer to the visitor) can't answer.
items.reference:
1. Browser cache
→
2. CDN edge
→
3. Origin

Why: a request only travels as far as it has to — each layer that answers removes load from every layer behind it.

items.prompt: The browser cache misses (no fresh copy) but the CDN edge cache hits. Does the origin server see this request?
choices: Yes, the origin always sees every request regardless of caching
No — the CDN edge answering the request means the origin is never contacted for it
Only if the visitor is more than 1,000 km from the origin
Only for the first request of the day
items.explanation: A cache hit at any layer stops the request from traveling further upstream. If the CDN edge has a fresh copy, it answers directly and the origin never sees that request at all — this is exactly how a CDN removes load from the origin, not just latency from the visitor.

Why: a request only travels as far as it has to — each layer that answers removes load from every layer behind it.

items.prompt: What is a 'cache miss'?
choices: A request that returns an error status code
A cache layer not having a fresh copy of the requested content, so it has to ask the next layer upstream
A visitor closing the browser tab before the response arrives
A cached copy that has been deleted by an administrator
items.explanation: A cache miss simply means that particular layer didn't have a fresh copy ready — it doesn't imply an error. The layer then asks whatever is upstream of it (another cache, or eventually the origin) and typically caches the result for next time.
items.reference:
✅ Hit

answered here

❌ Miss

ask upstream

Why: every miss that becomes a future hit is a request the origin no longer has to answer.

items.prompt: Which of these is a direct consequence of a high cache hit ratio?
choices: The origin server sees fewer requests, since more of them are answered by caches
Every visitor's page becomes permanently frozen at one version
TTLs are automatically extended to infinity
The CDN stops needing an origin at all
items.explanation: A cache hit means a layer answered the request without going further upstream. The more requests that get answered as hits (at any layer), the fewer requests reach the origin — that's the whole mechanism by which a CDN reduces origin load, not just latency.
items.reference:

Why: every miss that becomes a future hit is a request the origin no longer has to answer.

items.prompt: A CDN edge server receives a request for a URL it has never seen before. What does this produce?
choices: A cache hit, because the edge server assumes it's safe to answer
A cache miss — the edge server has no copy to serve, so it must fetch from upstream
An automatic error response to the visitor
A permanent block on that URL
items.explanation: With nothing cached for that URL yet, the edge server has no fresh copy to serve — that's a cache miss by definition, and it triggers a fetch from whatever is upstream (another cache layer, or the origin), typically caching the result afterward for future requests.

items.prompt: What does a cached response's TTL (time to live) control?
choices: How many visitors are allowed to request it
How long the cached copy is considered fresh before it must be re-validated or re-fetched
How large the file is allowed to be
Which country's edge servers are allowed to cache it
items.explanation: TTL is a duration — how long a cache is allowed to trust a stored copy as still-fresh without checking back with the origin. It has nothing to do with visitor counts, file size, or geography; it's purely about the freshness clock on one cached entry.
items.reference:
Short TTLfresher, more origin trips
Long TTLstaler, fewer origin trips

Why: TTL is a freshness clock on one cached entry — it trades staleness risk against origin load.

items.prompt: Content is cached with a very short TTL. What's the direct trade-off compared to a long TTL?
choices: Fresher content, but more requests reaching the origin to re-fetch it
Staler content, but fewer requests reaching the origin
No difference — TTL only affects browser caches, not CDNs
A short TTL makes the content uncacheable entirely
items.explanation: A short TTL means cached copies expire quickly, so caches have to go back to the origin more often — trading some origin load for fresher content. A long TTL is the opposite trade: less origin load, but a longer window where visitors could see stale content.
items.reference:
Short TTLfresher, more origin trips
Long TTLstaler, fewer origin trips

Why: TTL is a freshness clock on one cached entry — it trades staleness risk against origin load.

items.prompt: What makes the origin server different from every edge server in a CDN?
choices: The origin is just another cache, interchangeable with any edge server
The origin holds the authoritative, always-correct version of the data
The origin is only used for images, never for HTML
The origin is always physically located at the CDN vendor's headquarters
items.explanation: Every edge server holds a cached copy — a snapshot that's valid for a bounded time window. The origin is the one place holding the actual, current, authoritative data that every cached copy is ultimately a copy of.
items.reference:

authoritative
is copied by

🌍 Edges

Why: caching only makes sense relative to a single source of truth every copy is checked against.

items.prompt: If every edge server cache were wiped at once, what would still be true?
choices: All the site's data would be permanently lost
The origin still has the real data, so caches would simply refill from it on the next requests
The site would need to be rebuilt from scratch
Visitors would see a different site entirely
items.explanation: Caches only ever hold copies — losing all of them doesn't lose any real data, because the origin remains the authoritative source. The practical effect would be a temporary wave of cache misses (and origin load) while caches refill, not data loss.

items.prompt: Why can't a CDN just 'be' the origin and skip having a separate one?
choices: It could — origin and CDN are always the same physical machine
Because something has to be the single source of truth that all distributed edge copies are validated against
Because CDNs are not allowed to store any data at all
Because origins are always faster than edge servers
items.explanation: Caching only makes sense relative to a source of truth — something has to hold the real, current data that cached copies are checked against and refreshed from. That role is the origin's; a CDN without one would have no way to know what's actually correct when a cache expires or needs a purge.

items.prompt: A response includes Cache-Control: no-store. What must every cache do?
choices: Store it, but only for 60 seconds
Never store this response anywhere, period
Store it only if the visitor is on a mobile device
Store it exactly once and then delete it after the first reuse
items.explanation: no-store is the strictest directive — it forbids storing the response in any cache at all, not even the browser's own cache. It's meant for genuinely sensitive responses where even a private, single-use cache copy is unacceptable.
items.reference:
DirectiveMeans
publicany cache may store
privateonly the browser may store
no-cachemay store, must re-validate first
no-storenever store, anywhere
immutablenever changes, skip re-validation

Why: a cache only does what Cache-Control tells it — a misconfigured directive is an instruction, not a guess.

items.prompt: What does the immutable directive tell a cache?
choices: The response can never be requested again
This exact URL's content will never change, so there's no need to even re-validate on reload
The response must be re-fetched on every single request
The response is only valid for one specific visitor
items.explanation: immutable is a promise from the origin that the content behind this exact URL will never change — commonly paired with fingerprinted filenames (app.a1b2c3.js). It lets a cache skip even the lightweight re-validation check it would normally do on a page reload.
items.reference:
DirectiveMeans
publicany cache may store
privateonly the browser may store
no-cachemay store, must re-validate first
no-storenever store, anywhere
immutablenever changes, skip re-validation

Why: a cache only does what Cache-Control tells it — a misconfigured directive is an instruction, not a guess.

items.prompt: What's the difference between no-cache and no-store?
choices: They're synonyms — both forbid storing the response anywhere
no-cache allows storing it, but requires re-validating with the origin before reuse; no-store forbids storing it at all
no-cache only applies to CDNs, no-store only applies to browsers
no-cache means cache forever, no-store means never cache
items.explanation: Despite the confusing name, no-cache does not forbid caching — it allows a cache to store the response, but requires checking back with the origin (a lightweight revalidation) before serving it again. no-store is the stricter one that forbids storing it anywhere at all.
items.reference:

privateonly the browser may store
no-cachemay store, must re-validate first
no-storenever store, anywhere
immutablenever changes, skip re-validation

Why: a cache only does what Cache-Control tells it — a misconfigured directive is an instruction, not a guess.

items.prompt: A response is marked Cache-Control: private, max-age=600. Should a shared CDN edge cache store a copy for other visitors?
choices: Yes, because max-age=600 permits ten minutes of caching
No — private restricts caching to the requesting browser only, regardless of max-age
Yes, but only for the first 300 seconds
It depends on which country the CDN edge is in
items.explanation: private and max-age answer different questions: private says who may cache it (only the requesting browser, not any shared cache), while max-age only says how long a cache that's already permitted to store it should treat it as fresh. A CDN must respect private and not store a shared copy at all.
items.reference:
private

only this browser

public

any shared cache

Why: private/public answers WHO may cache; max-age only answers HOW LONG — the two are independent questions.

items.prompt: Why does mixing up public and private cause real security incidents in practice?
choices: It doesn't — the two directives are purely cosmetic and have no functional effect
A personalized response accidentally marked public can get cached by a shared CDN edge and served to a different visitor
public responses are always encrypted, private ones never are
private responses can only be served over HTTP, never HTTPS
items.explanation: If a response containing one user's personal data is mistakenly marked public (or left with no directive that a misconfigured CDN then treats as cacheable), a shared edge cache can store that response and serve it to a completely different visitor on their next matching request — exactly the leaky-cache-key failure mode covered in L3.
items.reference:
private

only this browser

public

any shared cache

Why: private/public answers WHO may cache; max-age only answers HOW LONG — the two are independent questions.

items.prompt: Why can a fingerprinted asset like app.a1b2c3.js be cached essentially forever?
choices: Because JavaScript files are always small
Because the filename itself changes whenever the content changes, so the same filename can never point at different content
Because browsers automatically expire JS files after a week regardless of headers
Because CDNs give JS files special treatment by default
items.explanation: Fingerprinting bakes a content hash into the filename, so any change to the file produces a new filename entirely. The old filename's content is therefore guaranteed never to change — there's no staleness risk to protect against, so an extremely long (or immutable) cache is safe.
items.reference:
Fingerprinted static — cache forever
Dynamic, shared — short TTL / stale-while-revalidate
Dynamic, personalized — no shared cache

Why: the right strategy tracks how often content changes and whether it's the same for everyone.

items.prompt: A logged-in user's shopping cart page should generally be handled how, at a shared CDN layer?
choices: Cached with a long TTL, same as static assets
Not cached at a shared layer at all — marked private or no-store, or served straight from the origin
Cached once and reused for every visitor to save origin load
Cached only during business hours
items.explanation: A shopping cart is dynamic and personalized — caching it at a shared layer risks showing one visitor's cart contents to another. Personalized responses generally need to bypass shared caching entirely, even at the cost of extra origin load.
items.reference:
Fingerprinted static — cache forever
Dynamic, shared — short TTL / stale-while-revalidate
Dynamic, personalized — no shared cache

Why: the right strategy tracks how often content changes and whether it's the same for everyone.

items.prompt: A public blog post's HTML changes rarely but not never. What's a reasonable strategy?
choices: Mark it no-store so it's always freshly generated
Cache it with a moderate TTL, or use stale-while-revalidate so visitors get a fast response while a background refresh keeps it from staying stale for long
Fingerprint the HTML filename the same way as JS assets
Never cache HTML, only images and scripts
items.explanation: Content that's the same for every visitor but occasionally changes is a good fit for caching with a bounded TTL, or stale-while-revalidate (serve the cached copy immediately, refresh it in the background) — getting most of caching's benefit without needing the content to be truly immutable.
items.reference:
Fingerprinted static — cache forever
Dynamic, shared — short TTL / stale-while-revalidate
Dynamic, personalized — no shared cache

Why: the right strategy tracks how often content changes and whether it's the same for everyone.

items.prompt: Compared to relying on a short TTL, what does purge-based invalidation trade away?
choices: Nothing — purge is strictly better in every way with no downside
Simplicity — the origin now has to know exactly what changed and explicitly tell every edge server to drop it
Freshness — purged content becomes staler, not fresher
It trades away the ability to cache the content at all
items.explanation: Purge-based invalidation buys freshness without needing a short TTL, but it costs complexity: the origin has to correctly identify what changed and fire a purge for exactly that content, reaching every relevant edge server. A short TTL needs none of that — it's simple, at the cost of a bounded window of staleness by default.
items.reference:
StrategyFreshnessComplexity
Short TTLbounded stalenesslow
Long TTL + purgefresh after purgehigher

Why: freshness without a short TTL isn't free — it costs the origin having to know exactly what changed.

items.prompt: A site sets an extremely long TTL and never purges anything. What's the practical risk?
choices: None — a long TTL always means better performance with no downside
Any content update won't be visible to visitors until the long TTL naturally expires
The origin will be overloaded with requests
The CDN will automatically shorten the TTL for you
items.explanation: A long TTL with no purge mechanism means staleness is bounded only by that long TTL — if the underlying content changes, visitors keep seeing the old version until the TTL naturally runs out. This is exactly why content that changes unpredictably usually needs either a shorter TTL or an active purge path.
items.reference:
StrategyFreshnessComplexity
Short TTLbounded stalenesslow
Long TTL + purgefresh after purgehigher

Why: freshness without a short TTL isn't free — it costs the origin having to know exactly what changed.

items.prompt: What is a cache key, in the context of a CDN?
choices: A password required to access cached content
What the CDN considers 'the same request' for caching purposes — by default usually the URL
An encryption key used to secure cached data at rest
A unique ID assigned to each visitor
items.explanation: The cache key determines which requests are treated as interchangeable for caching purposes — get it too narrow (missing something that should vary the response) and different content can collide under one cached entry; too wide, and identical content gets needlessly duplicated across many cache entries.
items.reference:
key = METHOD:URL[?vary-headers]
too narrow → different content collides
too wide → hit ratio drops

Why: the cache key decides what 'the same request' means — get it wrong and either content leaks or hit ratio collapses.

items.prompt: What problem does 'origin shielding' solve?
choices: It encrypts traffic between edge servers and the origin
It routes cache misses through one designated location first, so the origin sees at most one request per miss instead of one per edge PoP per miss
It automatically fixes bugs in origin server code
It prevents the origin from ever going offline
items.explanation: Without shielding, every one of potentially hundreds of edge PoPs could independently ask the origin for the same freshly-expired content at once. Origin shielding routes those misses through a single shield location first, so the origin sees far fewer duplicate requests for the same miss.
items.reference:
key = METHOD:URL[?vary-headers]
too narrow → different content collides
too wide → hit ratio drops

Why: the cache key decides what 'the same request' means — get it wrong and either content leaks or hit ratio collapses.

items.prompt: A cache key is built from the URL only, but the actual response also varies by Accept-Language header. What happens?
choices: Nothing — the cache automatically detects the language and adjusts
Visitors with different languages can be served a cached response generated for a different language than their own
The response will always be in English regardless of settings
The CDN will refuse to cache the response at all
items.explanation: If the cache key doesn't account for something that actually changes the response (like Accept-Language), the first language's response gets cached under a key that later requests for other languages will also match — serving the wrong language to those visitors. The fix is including that header in the cache key (via a Vary-style mechanism).
items.reference:
key = METHOD:URL[?vary-headers]
too narrow → different content collides
too wide → hit ratio drops

Why: the cache key decides what 'the same request' means — get it wrong and either content leaks or hit ratio collapses.

items.prompt: Implement buildCacheKey so it returns a cache key string in the form 'METHOD:URL' when there is no varyOn list (or it's empty) — no trailing '?'.

tests.description: no varyOn produces METHOD:URL with no trailing ?
POST method is reflected in the key

items.explanation: With no varyOn entries, varyPart is an empty string, so the template literal's conditional `${varyPart ? ... : ""}` contributes nothing and the key is exactly `METHOD:URL`. This is the common case — most requests don't need anything beyond the URL to identify a unique cacheable response.
items.reference:
buildCacheKey({method,url,varyOn,headers})
→ 'GET:/api/me'
→ 'GET:/api/me?accept-language=en'

Why: the cache key is exactly what makes two requests 'the same' for caching — everything else in the request is ignored.

items.prompt: Extend buildCacheKey so a single varyOn header (looked up case-insensitively in headers) is appended after a '?' as 'header=value'.

tests.description: single vary header is appended after ?
missing header value falls back to empty string, not undefined

items.explanation: The `?? ""` fallback matters: if a request is missing the varied-on header entirely, the key still has to be a well-formed string rather than containing the literal text 'undefined' — an unset header is treated as its own distinct, valid variant rather than crashing the key builder.
items.reference:
buildCacheKey({method,url,varyOn,headers})
→ 'GET:/api/me'
→ 'GET:/api/me?accept-language=en'

Why: the cache key is exactly what makes two requests 'the same' for caching — everything else in the request is ignored.

items.prompt: Extend buildCacheKey so multiple varyOn headers are appended sorted alphabetically by header name, joined with '&' — regardless of the order they appear in varyOn.

tests.description: two vary headers come out sorted regardless of input order
already-sorted order produces the same result

items.explanation: Sorting before joining guarantees the same set of varying headers always produces the exact same key string, no matter what order the caller happened to list them in varyOn. Without sorting, two logically identical requests could be assigned two different cache keys just because varyOn was ordered differently — silently destroying the hit ratio for no real reason.
items.reference:

Why: the cache key is exactly what makes two requests 'the same' for caching — everything else in the request is ignored.

items.prompt: Implement isFresh(storedAtMs, maxAgeMs, nowMs) — return true if the cached entry is still within its TTL window.

tests.description: well within TTL is fresh
well past TTL is not fresh

items.explanation: Freshness is purely a function of elapsed time versus the TTL: how long ago the entry was stored, compared to how long it's allowed to be trusted. Nothing about the content itself matters here — a cache doesn't re-inspect the body to decide freshness, only the clock.
items.reference:
isFresh(storedAt, maxAge, now)
→ (now - storedAt) < maxAge

Why: TTL freshness is purely a clock comparison — the cache never re-inspects content to decide.

items.prompt: Using the same isFresh(storedAtMs, maxAgeMs, nowMs), what should happen exactly at the boundary, when the elapsed time equals maxAgeMs exactly?

tests.description: exactly at the TTL boundary is NOT fresh (strict less-than)
one millisecond before the boundary is still fresh

items.explanation: Using strict less-than (not <=) means an entry exactly at its max-age boundary is already stale, not fresh — the TTL is treated as 'valid for less than maxAgeMs', not 'valid through maxAgeMs inclusive'. This avoids a class of off-by-one bugs where a request landing at the exact expiry millisecond gets served content that's already past its promised freshness window.
items.reference:
isFresh(storedAt, maxAge, now)
→ (now - storedAt) < maxAge

Why: TTL freshness is purely a clock comparison — the cache never re-inspects content to decide.

items.prompt: Using isFresh(storedAtMs, maxAgeMs, nowMs), verify the behavior when nowMs is before storedAtMs (a clock adjustment or bad input).

tests.description: now before storedAt still evaluates as fresh (negative elapsed < maxAge)
normal forward-time case still works

items.explanation: A negative elapsed time (now before storedAt) is still less than a positive maxAgeMs, so the simple subtraction naturally treats it as fresh — which is the safe default for an edge case that should essentially never happen with a well-behaved clock, rather than needing special-case handling that would only add complexity for a scenario that indicates a bigger problem (clock skew) elsewhere.
items.reference:
isFresh(storedAt, maxAge, now)
→ (now - storedAt) < maxAge

Why: TTL freshness is purely a clock comparison — the cache never re-inspects content to decide.

items.prompt: Implement parseCacheControl(header) returning { isPublic, maxAgeMs } from a Cache-Control header string like 'public, max-age=300'.

tests.description: public with max-age parses both fields
public with a larger max-age

items.explanation: The header is just a comma-separated list of directives as plain text — parsing it is string matching, not a structured format. max-age is always expressed in seconds in the header, so it has to be multiplied by 1000 to be usable alongside millisecond timestamps like Date.now().
items.reference:
parseCacheControl('public, max-age=300')
→ {isPublic:true, maxAgeMs:300000}

Why: a cache only stores a response when the origin's own header explicitly permits it — an absent or private header means don't store.

items.prompt: Using parseCacheControl(header), what should an empty or missing Cache-Control header ('') produce?

tests.description: empty header is not public and has 0 maxAgeMs

items.explanation: An origin that says nothing about caching is treated as opting out, not opting in — isPublic defaults to false and maxAgeMs to 0, so nothing gets stored. This mirrors the EdgeCache.get behavior from earlier in this level: absence of a caching instruction is the safer default of 'don't cache', not 'cache forever'.
items.reference:
parseCacheControl('public, max-age=300')
→ {isPublic:true, maxAgeMs:300000}

Why: a cache only stores a response when the origin's own header explicitly permits it — an absent or private header means don't store.

items.prompt: Using parseCacheControl(header), what should 'private, max-age=600' produce for isPublic?

tests.description: private with max-age is not public, but maxAgeMs is still parsed

items.explanation: isPublic only checks for the literal word 'public' — 'private, max-age=600' has a max-age but never the word 'public', so isPublic is correctly false. A shared cache reading this result would then know not to store the response, matching L2's rule that private overrides everything else about shared cacheability, regardless of what max-age says.
items.reference:
parseCacheControl('public, max-age=300')
→ {isPublic:true, maxAgeMs:300000}

Why: a cache only stores a response when the origin's own header explicitly permits it — an absent or private header means don't store.

items.prompt: Implement shouldFetchOrigin(key, inFlightKeys) — a Set-based helper that returns true (and registers the key) only for the FIRST concurrent request for a given key, modeling request coalescing without real async code.

tests.description: first request for a key triggers a fetch
the key ends up registered after the first call
tests.expr: const s = new Set(); shouldFetchOrigin('GET:/popular', s); expect(s.has('GET:/popular')).toBe(true)

items.explanation: The first caller for a key finds it absent, adds it, and gets true — it's the one responsible for actually fetching. Every other concurrent caller for that same key finds it already present and gets false, telling it to wait on the first caller's result instead of starting a duplicate origin fetch — this is the coalescing decision at the heart of avoiding a stampede.
items.reference:
shouldFetchOrigin(key, inFlightKeys)
1st caller → true (fetches)
2nd..Nth → false (rides the 1st)

Why: coalescing collapses N concurrent misses for the same key into exactly one origin fetch, avoiding a stampede.

items.prompt: Using shouldFetchOrigin(key, inFlightKeys), what should the SECOND concurrent request for the SAME key that's already in flight receive?

tests.description: second call for a key already in flight returns false
tests.expr: const s = new Set(['GET:/popular']); expect(shouldFetchOrigin('GET:/popular', s)).toBe(false)

tests.description: a different key is unaffected and still returns true
tests.expr: const s = new Set(['GET:/popular']); expect(shouldFetchOrigin('GET:/other', s)).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Once a key is already registered as in-flight, every subsequent request for that same key returns false without touching the set — those requests are meant to wait for the first one's result, not trigger their own redundant origin fetches. A completely different key is unrelated and still gets its own true on first sight, since coalescing only applies within the same cache key.
items.reference:
shouldFetchOrigin(key, inFlightKeys)
1st caller → true (fetches)
2nd..Nth → false (rides the 1st)

Why: coalescing collapses N concurrent misses for the same key into exactly one origin fetch, avoiding a stampede.

items.prompt: Implement getCacheStatus(now, storedAt, maxAgeMs, staleWhileRevalidateMs) returning 'FRESH' while inside the TTL window.

tests.description: well within maxAgeMs is FRESH
at the very start (age 0) is FRESH

items.explanation: FRESH is exactly the same freshness check as isFresh earlier in this level: the entry's age is still under its promised max-age, so it can be served with total confidence and no extra work needed.
items.reference:
FRESH — age < maxAge
STALE_WHILE_REVALIDATE — serve now, refresh in background
EXPIRED — must fetch before answering

Why: stale-while-revalidate adds a second window past maxAge where a slightly-old response is still good enough to serve immediately.

items.prompt: Using getCacheStatus, what should be returned when the entry is past maxAgeMs but still within the stale-while-revalidate window?

tests.description: just past maxAge but within the SWR window
near the end of the SWR window is still STALE_WHILE_REVALIDATE

items.explanation: The second window extends staleWhileRevalidateMs past the original maxAgeMs boundary — during that extra window, the entry is old enough that a background refresh should be kicked off, but not so old that it's unsafe to serve immediately while that refresh happens. This is exactly what avoids making every visitor wait on the origin at the TTL boundary, as covered in the stampede discussion above.
items.reference:
FRESH — age < maxAge
STALE_WHILE_REVALIDATE — serve now, refresh in background
EXPIRED — must fetch before answering

Why: stale-while-revalidate adds a second window past maxAge where a slightly-old response is still good enough to serve immediately.

items.prompt: Using getCacheStatus, what should be returned once the entry is past BOTH maxAgeMs and the stale-while-revalidate window?

tests.description: past both windows is EXPIRED
a fresh-again entry with a later storedAt is FRESH, not EXPIRED

items.explanation: Once age exceeds both maxAgeMs and the extra staleWhileRevalidateMs window, the entry is too old to serve at all — a request must actually wait on a fresh origin fetch before it can be answered. The second test shows this status resets cleanly once storedAt is updated by a real refresh, which is exactly what a background revalidation is supposed to accomplish.
